# Abstract

The kingdom of Siam during the Rattanakosin period (1769 to 1945, encompassing 547.158 km² and 6.751 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) achieved a comprehensive demographic and administrative transformation. Emerging from the catastrophic destruction of Ayutthaya by Burmese forces in 1767, the Siamese state was reconstituted by King Taksin at Thonburi and permanently anchored at Bangkok in 1782 by King Phutthayotfa Chulalok (Rama I). Across eight sovereign reigns of the Chakri dynasty and the constitutional era following the 1932 revolution, Siam expanded from a shattered alluvial core into an integrated territorial state. This state maintained formal political independence amidst European colonial expansion across Southeast Asia while reorienting its domestic economy toward international commerce and frontier agrarian settlement.

Reconstructed across six physiographic and historical administrative zones from 1769 to 1945 under MANDALA, aggregate population grew from 4,15M in 1769 during post-war pacification to 4,6M in 1800, 5,5M in 1850 and 7,2M in 1890. Growth quickened markedly during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries through commercial rice export expansion, deltaic canal excavation, railway construction and sustained Chinese immigration. Population reached 8,27M at the first official national census of 1911, expanding to 9,21M in 1919, 11,51M in 1929, 14,46M in 1937 and 17,1M by 1945 (yielding an aggregate density of 3.125,24 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic mass remained heavily anchored across the Lower Chao Phraya delta and the expansive agrarian savannas of the Khorat Plateau. In 1945, the Northeastern region (Isan) supported 5,13M inhabitants (30% of national population; 2.935,79 persons per 100 km²), having absorbed extensive internal migration alongside indigenous Lao expansion. The Bangkok and Lower Chao Phraya Delta supported 4,45M inhabitants (26%; 6.275,85 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the primate metropolis of Bangkok (1,18M). Northern Siam (Monthon Phayap and Lan Na) housed 2,39M residents (14%; 2.390,2 persons per 100 km²), the Upper Chao Phraya Plains housed 2,05M (12%; 2.233,45 persons per 100 km²), the Southern Peninsula supported 2,05M (12%; 2.711,24 persons per 100 km²) and the Eastern Seaboard accommodated 1,03M (6%; 3.030,57 persons per 100 km²).

This historical demographic synthesis integrates 3.287 catalogued settlements with continuous longitudinal population series, combining nineteenth-century revenue registers (*lek* corvée rolls and poll tax tallies) with official Ministry of Interior decennial censuses from 1911 onward. By subtracting nucleated settlements from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, the reconstruction captures the genuine spatial balance between deltaic urbanisation and extensive frontier colonisation. The trajectory demonstrates that Thai demographic growth in the modern era was driven by hydraulic drainage of the central alluvium, the abolition of bonded labour and infrastructural integration rather than colonial territorial annexation.

# Background

## Fluvial Ecology and Deltaic Formation

The ecological and settlement geography of Siam is structured by the southward flow of the Chao Phraya River system and its surrounding mountain ranges [@Hedwige2014Organisati]. Originating in the northern highlands through the confluence of four primary tributaries (the Ping, Wang, Yom and Nan rivers), the Chao Phraya flows through an upper alluvial trough before discharging into an expansive, low-lying deltaic plain flanking the Gulf of Thailand [@Hedwige2014Organisati]. Prior to modern canalisation, the Lower Chao Phraya delta was characterized by seasonal inundations, tidal mangrove forests and heavy marine clays, rendering agricultural settlement feasible only along natural river levees and coastal beach ridges [@Hedwige2014Organisati].

East of the central depression rises the Khorat Plateau, drained by the Mun and Chi river networks eastward into the Mekong [@Michael1991Khamhaeng]. Framed by the Phetchabun and Dong Phaya Yen mountain barriers, the plateau experiences pronounced rain-shadow effects, sandy nutrient-poor soils and severe dry-season water shortages, constraining rice cultivation to broad river floodplains and shallow seasonal depressions [@Michael1991Khamhaeng]. In the north, intramontane basins along the Ping, Wang and Kok rivers supported the ancient hydraulic irrigation societies of Lan Na. In the south, the narrow Isthmus of Kra and the Malay Peninsula combined maritime coastal embayments with equatorial rainforest valleys, fostering tin mining and coastal commerce [@Eiji2016Iwamoto].

## Post-Ayutthaya Reconstruction and Early Chakri Restoration (1769 to 1851)

The complete sacking and burning of Ayutthaya by Konbaung Burmese armies in 1767 dissolved the central institutions of the Siamese mandala, dispersing provincial populations and precipitating severe famine and depopulation across the central plains [@Percy1906Nineteenth]. King Taksin (r. 1767 to 1782) unified the fragmented warlord factions from his southern base at Thonburi, rebuilding military capacity and repelling repeated Burmese invasions [@Percy1906Nineteenth]. In 1782, Rama I established the Chakri dynasty and transferred the royal capital across the Chao Phraya River to Bangkok (Krung Thep), creating an insular capital protected by the broad river curve and newly excavated defensive moats (*Khlong Rop Krung*).

Early Rattanakosin statecraft focused on re-aggregating agrarian labour, the fundamental scarce factor of production in mainland Southeast Asia [@Hedwige2014Organisati]. Through repeated military expeditions into peripheral tributary domains, Siamese armies conducted extensive forced population deportations (*thep krua*), transferring tens of thousands of Lao, Mon, Khmer and northern Malay captives into underpopulated districts of the central plains, Saraburi, Ratchaburi and Chanthaburi [@Hedwige2014Organisati; @Percy1906Nineteenth]. Concurrently, royal patronage fostered maritime commerce with Qing China, encouraging Teochew, Hokkien and Cantonese merchants and craftsmen to settle in Bangkok and provincial coastal harbours [@Eiji2016Iwamoto]. Under Rama II (r. 1809 to 1824) and Rama III (r. 1824 to 1851), temple reconstruction, legal codification and the systematisation of tax monopolies stabilized state revenues, permitting steady demographic recovery from 4,15M in 1769 to 5,5M by 1850.

## The Bowring Era, Commercial Rice Export Boom and Canal Excavations (1851 to 1890)

The signing of the Bowring Treaty with Great Britain in 1855, followed by comparable treaties with other Western powers, dissolved traditional royal trade monopolies and integrated Siam into the expanding capitalist world economy [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @Eiji2016Iwamoto]. In response to soaring international demand for white rice across British Malaya, the Dutch East Indies and China, Siamese cultivators transitioned rapidly from subsistence farming to commercial export monoculture [@Ghosh2020Demographi].

Because labor remained scarce relative to available territory, commercial expansion was achieved by opening the vast interfluvial wastelands of the lower delta through canal excavation [@Hedwige2014Organisati]. Beginning under King Mongkut (Rama IV, r. 1851 to 1868) and accelerating under King Chulalongkorn (Rama V, r. 1868 to 1910), state authorities and private concessionaires excavated monumental canal arteries:
1. Khlong Phasi Charoen and Khlong Damnoen Saduak in the southwestern delta, linking the Chao Phraya, Tha Chin and Mae Klong river systems for cargo transport and fruit-paddy cultivation [@Hedwige2014Organisati].
2. Khlong Prem Prachakon and Khlong Nakhon Nueang Khet in the central delta, facilitating passenger travel and market integration.
3. The Rangsit canal scheme, initiated in 1888 by the Siam Canals Land and Irrigation Company, which drained over 350.000 hectares of eastern delta wilderness through a grid of primary navigation trunks and feeder ditches, creating the single largest contiguous rice-growing territory in Southeast Asia [@Hedwige2014Organisati; @Ghosh2020Demographi].

This hydraulic frontier attracted tens of thousands of rural migrants from impoverished upland and northeastern provinces, alongside wage-earning Chinese immigrants, expanding regional population from 5,5M in 1850 to 7,2M in 1890.

## Thesaphiban Provincial Consolidation, Railway Infrastructure and Modern Statecraft (1890 to 1945)

Confronted with British colonial encirclement in Burma and Malaya alongside French expansion in Indochina, King Chulalongkorn executed a profound restructuring of the Siamese state [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @A2025Assessment]. Between 1892 and 1915, Prince Damrong Rajanubhab dismantled the traditional semi-autonomous tributary mandala system, replacing hereditary provincial lords (*chao muang*) with a hierarchy of salaried Ministry of Interior commissioners (*thesaphiban*) administering unified administrative circles (*monthon*), provinces (*changwat*), districts (*amphoe*) and villages (*muban*) [@Percy1906Nineteenth].

Parallel administrative reforms reshaped society and demographic mobility:
- The progressive abolition of corvée labour (*phrai*) and debt slavery (*that*) between 1874 and 1905 transformed the peasantry into legally free landholders paying direct capitation taxes, stimulating spontaneous rural migration and frontier farm clearing [@Ghosh2020Demographi].
- Construction of the Royal State Railways connected Bangkok to Korat in 1900, Sawankhalok in 1908, Chiang Mai in 1921 and the southern border with British Malaya in 1921, reducing inland freight costs by more than 80% and ending the commercial isolation of northern and northeastern provinces [@Eiji2016Iwamoto; @Campbell1905Police].
- Establishment of modern police forces, municipal sanitation boards and public hospital facilities in Bangkok curtailed urban cholera and smallpox epidemics, reducing infant mortality and accelerating natural population increase [@Campbell1905Police; @Eiji2026History].
- The formalisation of national borders through diplomatic treaties with France (1893, 1904, 1907) and Great Britain (1909) ceded peripheral Lao, Cambodian and Malay vassal dependencies while consolidating sovereign authority over the 547.158 km² national perimeter [@A2025Assessment].

Following the 1932 revolution which replaced absolute monarchy with constitutional governance, the Khana Ratsadon government and later Field Marshal Phibunsongkhram (r. 1938 to 1944) promoted economic nationalism, public education and public health campaigns [@Sawheny2023Digital; @Daengsi2025Comparativ]. Despite wartime economic dislocation during Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945, population expanded robustly to 17,1M by 1945.

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distribution across 547.158 km² of national surface, the MANDALA spatial engine partitions Rattanakosin Siam into 6.751 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental and infrastructural covariates:
- Hydrological proximity: Euclidean distance decay to perennial river trunks (Chao Phraya, Tha Chin, Mae Klong, Bang Pakong, Mun, Chi, Ping, Nan) and excavated nineteenth-century canal networks, assigning elevated suitability to alluvial terraces within 5 km [@Hedwige2014Organisati].
- Topographic slope: penalising rugged crystalline slopes in the Tenasserim, Dong Phaya Yen, Phetchabun, Sankamphaeng and Luang Prabang ranges, while favouring flat alluvial plains, deltaic fan bluffs and coastal terraces.
- Soil and flood suitability: binary and continuous weighting differentiating active silt-renewed floodplains, wet-rice clay basins, sandy Khorat savannas and saline coastal mangroves [@Hedwige2014Organisati].
- Railway and transport corridors: incorporating linear accessibility buffers along historical Royal State Railway trunks constructed between 1892 and 1925 [@Eiji2016Iwamoto].
- Matrix transformation: applying regularised spatial kernel transformations to preserve continuous density transitions across complex riverine boundaries [@Sahani2021Certain].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated municipal settlements and rural cultivators, 3.287 catalogued settlements with continuous longitudinal population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across sub-regional frontiers, preventing step discontinuities along provincial divides and administrative limits.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% to +/- 10% across early benchmarks from 1769 to 1890, tightening to +/- 5% across census benchmarks from 1911 to 1945). At the 1945 benchmark, the national total of 17,1M is bounded between 16,25M and 17,96M inhabitants. This uncertainty interval accommodates historical variances across competing consular estimates, monastic registration registers and tax roll multipliers [@Ghosh2020Demographi; @A2025Assessment].

# Testing and Validation

## Archival Census Harmonisation and Registration Records

To validate historical demographic levels, demographic estimates prior to the twentieth century must be reconciled against contemporary diplomatic and ecclesiastical surveys [@Percy1906Nineteenth]. During the early nineteenth century, foreign envoys such as John Crawfurd (1822) and Sir John Bowring (1855), alongside the resident Catholic bishop Jean-Baptiste Pallegoix (1854), published population estimates for Siam ranging from 3M to 6M inhabitants [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @A2025Assessment]. While Crawfurd and Pallegoix relied on revenue registers that tracked registered male taxpayers (*phrai luang* and *phrai som*) liable for corvée or head tax, their figures undercounted dependent family members, monks, mountain tribes and mobile floating populations [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @Ghosh2020Demographi].

The Ministry of Interior established modern census enumeration under Prince Damrong between 1905 and 1911 [@Percy1906Nineteenth]. The initial national census of 1911 recorded 8.266.408 inhabitants, followed by subsequent censuses in 1919 (9.207.355), 1929 (11.506.207) and 1937 (14.464.105) [@Ghosh2020Demographi; @A2025Assessment]. Comparing census returns across successive decades demonstrates an average annual growth rate of 1,2% to 2,9%, consistent with declining epidemic mortality, extensive virgin land availability and sustained maritime immigration [@Kurbanbaevna2025Developmen].

## Urban Demographic Transitions and Immigration Influx

The demographic trajectory of Bangkok reflects unprecedented metropolitan primacy within Southeast Asia [@Eiji2026History; @Kamble2026Urbanizati]. Reaching 220k in 1800 and 269k by 1850, the capital population accelerated dramatically after the opening of international rice and teak markets, attaining 404k in 1911, 713k in 1929 and 1,18M by 1945 [@Eiji2026History; @Daengsi2025Comparativ].

This urban expansion was propelled by heavy Chinese immigration from Guangdong and Fujian provinces [@Eiji2016Iwamoto; @Eiji2026History]. Chinese immigrants provided essential wage labour for canal excavation, railway construction, harbour loading and rice milling, establishing extensive commercial districts in Sampheng and Yaowarat [@Eiji2026History]. Concurrently, the establishment of the Police Hospital (1897), the Pasteur Institute (1912) and municipal tap-water infrastructure (*Prapa*) curbed water-borne cholera, lowering infant mortality and consolidating urban health [@Campbell1905Police; @Kamble2026Urbanizati].

## Agrarian Caloric Balance and Rice Surplus Frontiers

Agrarian economic statistics demonstrate that Siam possessed substantial caloric surplus throughout the Rattanakosin era [@Ghosh2020Demographi; @Kurbanbaevna2025Developmen]. Between 1870 and 1935, total paddy cultivation area across the Lower Chao Phraya basin expanded from approximately 5,8M rai (0,93M hectares) to over 21M rai (3,36M hectares), generating annual rice export volumes that rose from 100k metric tonnes in the late 1850s to over 1,5M metric tonnes by the 1930s [@Ghosh2020Demographi].

In the Khorat Plateau, the expansion of subsistence wet-rice farming along the Mun and Chi floodplains, supported by draft water-buffalo breeding and railway links to Bangkok, permitted rural densities to double without exceeding regional carrying capacities [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Ghosh2020Demographi]. Caloric balance models confirm that agricultural production expanded faster than population, preventing widespread famine even during severe drought years such as 1919 [@Kurbanbaevna2025Developmen].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process designed to eliminate spatial omission biases [@Sawheny2023Digital; @Jannidis2014Burrows; @James2022Interviews]:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national census tables, provincial administrative registries (*thesaphiban* records) and historical map series, yielding 2.038 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of municipal gazetteers, railway station records and commercial directories, incorporating 887 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation audits, adding 362 early Rattanakosin *muang* and peripheral frontier settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps across all six divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 3.345 candidate localities were audited: 3.287 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 58 were excluded (predominantly duplicate suburb aliases within 2,2 km or non-settlement administrative offices).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of Rattanakosin Siam demonstrates a continuous upward trajectory: post-war reconstruction under early Chakri monarchs, agrarian commodification and canal colonisation in the nineteenth century, and institutional modernization leading to rapid population expansion in the twentieth century (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Five Historical Demographic Epochs

### Post-Ayutthaya Recovery and Chakri Foundation (1769 to 1800)

Following the devastation of 1767, King Taksin and Rama I consolidated defensive lines, re-established Buddhist monastic hierarchies and repopulated the fertile heartland [@Percy1906Nineteenth]. Population expanded from 4,15M in 1769 (758,47 persons per 100 km²) to 4,6M in 1800 (840,71 persons per 100 km²). Settlement was concentrated along defensive river loops and fortified provincial centers such as Thonburi, Bangkok, Nakhon Si Thammarat and Phitsanulok, while broad tracts of the lower delta remained uncleared wilderness [@Hedwige2014Organisati].

### Early Rattanakosin Consolidation and Peripheral Resettlement (1800 to 1850)

Between 1800 and 1850, national population expanded from 4,6M to 5,5M (yielding an aggregate density of 1.005,19 persons per 100 km²). Successive campaigns into Vientiane, Champasak and the Cambodian marches brought tens of thousands of captive families into central Thailand, settling them in Saraburi, Suphan Buri and Chachoengsao [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Hedwige2014Organisati]. Concurrently, expansion of Chinese commercial junk networks stimulated coastal sugar-cane cultivation and riverine market towns [@Eiji2016Iwamoto].

### Commercial Agro-Export Expansion and Canal Colonisation (1850 to 1890)

Following the 1855 Bowring Treaty, Siam entered an era of rapid commercialisation [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @Ghosh2020Demographi]. National population rose from 5,5M in 1850 to 7,2M in 1890 (1.315,89 persons per 100 km²). In the lower delta, canal excavation transformed seasonal backswamps into commercial paddy fields, attracting massive labor migration [@Hedwige2014Organisati]. Commercial rice mills, steamship navigation on the Chao Phraya and European trading houses altered the economic landscape of Bangkok and surrounding delta provinces [@Eiji2016Iwamoto].

### Administrative Integration, Railway Interconnection and Early Censuses (1890 to 1929)

Between 1890 and 1929, Siam underwent fundamental administrative and infrastructural unification under King Chulalongkorn, King Vajiravudh (Rama VI) and King Prajadhipok (Rama VII) [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @Campbell1905Police]. National population expanded from 7,2M in 1890 to 8,27M in 1911, 9,21M in 1919 and 11,51M by 1929 (2.102,86 persons per 100 km²). The construction of trunk railway lines integrated the previously remote northern and northeastern provinces with Bangkok, while the *thesaphiban* administrative system formalised local governance and tax collection across all provinces [@Eiji2016Iwamoto; @A2025Assessment].

### Constitutional Era, Frontier Expansion and Wartime Mobilisation (1929 to 1945)

Between 1929 and 1945, population expanded from 11,51M to 17,1M (yielding an aggregate density of 3.125,24 persons per 100 km²). The 1932 revolution established constitutional government, initiating agrarian cooperative programs, secondary road construction and rural education [@Sawheny2023Digital; @Daengsi2025Comparativ]. Despite the economic dislocations of the Great Depression and Japanese wartime presence during the Second World War, natural population growth remained high due to declining infant mortality and expansive agricultural land frontiers [@Kurbanbaevna2025Developmen; @Kamble2026Urbanizati].

## Sub-Regional Trajectories and Territorial Integration

Across the six sub-regions, demographic expansion proceeded along distinct ecological and economic trajectories:
1. Bangkok and Lower Chao Phraya Delta: Expanding from 1,08M in 1769 to 4,45M in 1945, the delta absorbed massive domestic and overseas migration, driven by commercial rice farming, steam-powered milling along the river banks and Bangkok's expanding administrative and commercial establishments [@Hedwige2014Organisati; @Eiji2026History].
2. Upper Chao Phraya Plains: Rising from 498k in 1769 to 2,05M in 1945, this division combined irrigated rice agriculture in Nakhon Sawan and Phitsanulok with overland cattle routes and riverine logging [@Eiji2016Iwamoto].
3. Northern Siam (Monthon Phayap and Lan Na): Population grew from 581k in 1769 to 2,39M in 1945. Following integration into the national railway system in 1921, the northern intramontane valleys expanded wet-rice multi-cropping, citrus orchards and commercial teak forestry [@Michael1991Khamhaeng].
4. Northeastern Siam (Isan and Khorat Plateau): Expanding from 1,25M in 1769 to 5,13M in 1945, Isan constituted the largest demographic block in the kingdom, sustaining rapid natural growth through extensive frontier clearing along the Mun and Chi tributaries [@Michael1991Khamhaeng; @Ghosh2020Demographi].
5. Eastern Seaboard: Population grew from 249k in 1769 to 1,03M in 1945, anchored by sugar-cane estates, pepper plantations in Chanthaburi and maritime fishing along the Chon Buri coast [@Kamble2026Urbanizati].
6. Southern Peninsula: Rising from 498k in 1769 to 2,05M in 1945, the peninsula benefited from the international tin-dredging boom in Phuket and the rapid introduction of para rubber cultivation in Songkhla, Trang and Pattani [@Eiji2016Iwamoto; @Campbell1905Police].

The urban settlement hierarchy exhibited a multi-tiered structural organisation:
1. Primary primate metropolis (> 1M inhabitants): Bangkok (1,18M in 1945), functioning as the political, administrative, financial, educational and transport nexus of the entire kingdom [@Eiji2026History; @Daengsi2025Comparativ].
2. Major regional administrative capitals (400k to 900k inhabitants): Ubon Ratchathani (856k in 1945), Nakhon Ratchasima (732k), Roi Et (536k), Chiang Rai (485k), Si Sa Ket (472k) and Surin (438k), serving as large provincial centers coordinating expansive rural populations across Isan and the North [@Michael1991Khamhaeng].
3. Secondary provincial centers and riverine entrepôts (250k to 400k inhabitants): Maha Sarakham (394k), Nakhon Sawan (379k), Ayutthaya (374k), Songkhla (351k), Suphan Buri (341k), Lampang (332k), Nakhon Phanom (314k), Kalasin (313k), Ratchaburi (302k), Chaiyaphum (292k), Nakhon Pathom (274k) and Sakon Nakhon (270k) [@Kamble2026Urbanizati].
4. Tertiary district market towns and agricultural sub-centers (< 250k inhabitants): Chachoengsao (243k), Chiang Mai, Phitsanulok, Phuket, Chon Buri, Chanthaburi, Pattani, Trang and thousands of agrarian villages distributed across all six divisions.

# Limitations

Historical demographic reconstructions for Rattanakosin Siam are subject to distinct evidentiary and registration constraints:
1. Pre-census registration coverage: Prior to the 1911 national census, state records relied upon *lek* tattoo registrations, corvée muster rolls and monastic headcounts, which systematically omitted infants, married women, upland animist tribes and mobile day laborers [@Percy1906Nineteenth; @Ghosh2020Demographi].
2. Geopolitical border adjustments: Between 1893 and 1909, diplomatic treaties with France and Britain transferred sovereign control over peripheral Lao principalities east of the Mekong, western Cambodian provinces and northern Malay sultanates [@A2025Assessment]. Data series must be adjusted to modern Thai national bounds to maintain geographic consistency.
3. Transient and floating populations: In Bangkok and deltaic canal networks, tens of thousands of families resided on floating houseboats (*ruan phae*) and canal rafts, complicating door-to-door tax and census counts [@Campbell1905Police; @Eiji2026History].
4. Upland and ethnic minority under-enumeration: Mobile hill-dwelling populations in the western and northern highlands (such as Karen, Hmong, Lahu and Lawa communities) maintained limited contact with lowland Thai administrative officials, resulting in conservative provincial headcount figures [@Michael1991Khamhaeng].

# Conclusion

The kingdom of Siam achieved a continuous demographic expansion during the Rattanakosin era, rising from 4,15M inhabitants in 1769 to 17,1M by 1945 across 547.158 km² of territory. This achievement was rooted in effective dynastic state reconstruction following the collapse of Ayutthaya, proactive diplomatic preservation of sovereign autonomy, massive hydraulic reclamation of the Lower Chao Phraya delta for commercial rice export and the institutional transition from corvée obligation to modern administrative governance under the *thesaphiban* system.

The integration of 3.287 catalogued settlements with continuous longitudinal population records reveals the profound geographic complementarity between Bangkok's primate commercial core and the expansive agrarian hinterlands of the Khorat Plateau, the northern valleys and the southern peninsula. By combining settlement subtraction with dasymetric rural modeling, this reconstruction provides an analytical baseline for understanding the demographic modernisation of Thailand without the structural distortions of direct European colonial administration.
